utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The examination by Mr. Fila will now continue. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration which you made at the beginning of your evidence to tell the truth will continue to apply to your evidence today. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jovanovic, yesterday, we spoke about the SPS Working Group in Kosovo, and you said that, after the completion of the anti-terrorist operation, they returned to Belgrade. I was just about to ask you this question. I'm afraid I may have forgotten it. I know now. Did any of the team members remain in Kosovo and Metohija? Did any of them stay back: Minic, Matkovic, and Andjelkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that. Zoran Andjelkovic stayed back in Kosovo and Metohija. He did not remain in Kosmet in his capacity as a member of that team but as the president of the Provisional Executive Board for Kosovo and Metohija. He had been appointed to this post by the national assembly of the Republic of Serbia. While he performed this function, he was not in his capacity as a member of the SPS team.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: There are people here who don't come from our country. Could you explain this term "Provisional Executive Board" or "Provisional Executive Council"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Provisional Executive Council is an executive body of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija. It was established in order to help normalise relations in Kosovo and Metohija. Its mandate was a restricted one. It was about achieving a political solution. It was about holding a democratic election which was to take place under the supervision of the OSCE. After the election, all the bodies of self-government in Kosovo and Metohija were to be constituted; the executive bodies, the judicial bodies, and a whole series of political institutions, the kind normally envisaged by any form of self-government.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let's go back to the SPS team. Speaking of that team, the three persons, Minic, Matkovic, and Andjelkovic, could you tell us how the team was organised?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The team was organised in the same way as various other teams that the SPS would sometimes organise. Milomir Minic was formally in charge of the team. He was, in formal terms, the head of the team. His job was to coordinate any actions taken by the team and to keep in touch with the party headquarters of the SPS. However, his position can only be defined in conditional terms. There was no practical chain of command within that team. Milomir was "primus inter pares." Although the team acted jointly, there were spheres of activity that individual members of that team were more or less in charge of. Milomir Minic, for example, was in charge of contact with the various party bodies in Kosovo and Metohija and also in charge of maintaining relations with the Main Board of the party back in Belgrade. The job of the other member of the team, Zoran Andjelkovic, had to do with daily contact with the citizens, meaning not just people working for the SPS, but, rather, citizens throughout Kosovo and Metohija. His role was it to encourage dialogue among them, to encourage them to talk to one another, to point out the need for a political solution through talks at all levels. His role was also to explain that this was not only in the realm of political talks in Pristina and Belgrade but had to occur further afield as well. The third member of the team, Dusan Matkovic, was in charge of dealing with people from the local economy. The objective of these activities was to start up production in some of the companies and to generally improve the functioning of the economy in Kosmet throughout. This would be, in very rough terms, how work was organised within this team of three.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In your opinion - and you did hold a post that you held in Belgrade, after all - how did this team keep in touch with the party headquarters in Belgrade in order to keep them up-to-date?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the responsibility of this team, and this is something that had been decided by the Main Board. I know that the team was permanently in touch with the Main Board and the Executive Board. The head of the team, Milomir Minic, entertained daily contact by phone with the secretary of the Executive Board. They even spoke several times a day sometimes. He would convey to him all kinds of information from Kosovo and Metohija regarding the situation on the ground, as it were. He told him about the expectations and requests of the citizens and party activists. He would also convey information about any current action being taken by the team in various places in Kosovo and Metohija. Another thing I know is that the remaining two members of the team, Andjelkovic and Matkovic, were permanently in touch with the Executive Board of the Socialist Party of Serbia in Belgrade, and they also kept them up-to-date with everything that their jobs comprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I forgot to ask you about this earlier. We know that Slobodan Milosevic was the President of the SPS, but you keep mentioning the Secretary-General. We haven't mentioned this person's name yet, have we?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name is Gorica Gajevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please set matters right on the transcript. It should read Gorica Gajevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you now please open the binder that's in front of you, sir. This is tab 2, Defence Exhibit 2D53. Mr. Jovanovic, these are minutes from a meeting of the SPS Executive Board. The date is the 11th of September, 1998. Could you please, first of all, confirm if that is true? Is that the record? Are these the minutes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are minutes. I recognise the form. I recognise the stamp. I recognise the signature of the Secretary-General. These are minutes taken at a meeting of the Executive Board of the SPS.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you please have a close look now, and then go to page 2. Very carefully look at III, paragraph one. Have a close look, please, and please explain. Please explain, first of all, what this is all about. Don't read back. We're all perfectly able to read. Please just comment.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This meeting of the Executive Board took place on the 11th of September, 1998. It was devoted to a range of different subjects. As for the situation in Kosovo and Metohija, issues to do with humanitarian aid were reviewed at the meeting, aid for the citizens living in this province. It was quite clear that the objective of ongoing terrorist activity was to make life impossible for citizens in as many different municipalities as possible throughout Kosovo and Metohija. The terrorists laid siege to roads in order to cut the supply lines through most of the province, expelling many of the citizens from their homes; therefore, these people that had been expelled needed practically everything they could get. The objective of the terrorists was to cause chaos and to prevent people from remaining in their homes or habitats so that they themselves might be able to exercise better control over the territory. It was for this reason that the SPS established a special fund for providing humanitarian aid to people in this part of our republic. Secretary-General Gorica Gajevic was the president of this fund.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, was the aid provided to members of the SPS in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can explain that. Aid was provided to all those who were in need, regardless of their party affiliation; that is, them being or not being members of the SPS. That wasn't taken into account, and also regardless of their ethnicity. The SPS, in terms of its political platform, was a party of Serbia citizens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've answered my question. What proportion of the population, the adult population, of Kosovo were members of the SPS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If my recollection is accurate, we had about 35.000 members in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what was the amount of the fund for humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The entire party organisation was involved in collecting humanitarian aid. All of our municipal boards across Serbia were involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the total amount of money raised and distributed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're looking at something to the tune of several tens of millions of dinars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you not have an accurate figure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last figure that I remember is 168 million dinars, but not all of the assistance was money. There was aid in kind; namely, clothes, footwear, food, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And over what period of time was this aid provided?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This aid was provided most intensively during the month of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then it continued during the months after of that. What I wanted to say was, actually, that we coordinated this humanitarian activity with other organisations, like the Red Cross and many other non-governmental humanitarian organisations, both from home and abroad, that were active in Kosmet. Furthermore, if I may proceed, this aid was distributed through about ten outposts in Kosovo and Metohija, and it constituted significant support for the citizens, not only in terms of normalising life itself, but also as a clear expression of the fact that state and political structures would not leave them on their own and forget about their suffering that was caused by the terrorists with a view to attaining their separatist objectives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understood everything until the very last part of your answer. I thought the point you were making was that the SPS humanitarian aid was not part of the state structure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So how did that demonstrate that the state structure would not abandon the people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I wanted to say was that when giving humanitarian aid, we cooperated with all other organisations. In addition to the state structures, there were political structures in Kosovo that were also active. This kind of an expression of support for the citizens was supposed to mean that the entire republic was standing by them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In order to fully clarify this matter, in paragraph 2 of what you have in front of you, there is a particular person who is mentioned, Vojislav Zivkovic, and he seems to be saying something there. Would you give us, roughly, a comment in terms of where humanitarian aid was being distributed and to who and how and so on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vojislav Zivkovic was president of the Provincial Board of the Socialist Party of Serbia in Kosovo and Metohija. Here, at this particular session, he informed this detail about the types of assistance provided, how it was distributed, to who, and through 12 different localities at that; that is to say, that humanitarian aid did not only flow into the centre of the province, it was equally distributed to the areas where it was needed the most. The organisation of providing humanitarian aid was set up along the lines of providing what was really needed. Our Provincial Board contacted with other boards throughout Serbia and sent lists in terms of what was needed the most. I have to say that the documentation about the work of the fund was destroyed, unfortunately, during the rocket attacks aimed at the headquarters of the Main Board of the Socialist Party of Serbia during the NATO aggression, so I'm not in a position to provide precise information.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let us just deal with something that is going to be important later. You have just given a name, Vojislav Zivkovic. Is that the same person who was in Rambouillet who signed the documents that we will be discussing later on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's one and the same person. In Rambouillet -- he was in Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was his position there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the representative of the ethnic community of the Serbs from Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to ask you to look at tab 3. The number is 2D56. That is the minutes of the Executive Board meeting of the SPS held on the 22nd of September, 1998. Could you please first confirm to me that this document is authentic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by its form, the signature, and the stamp, the signature of Gorica Gajevic, Secretary-General, this is an authentic document, minutes from a session of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please look at page 2, paragraph 1 now. Please take a careful look. Use all the time you need. That's no problem. Tell us when you're ready.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My question is: Who made the introductory statement, and what was discussed there? Please don't read anything to us, just tell us in your own words.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The introductory statement was made by Milomir Minic as head of the team for Kosovo and Metohija. The essence of his statement was, actually, a report on the activities of the team and the implementation of the conclusions reached by the Main Board at its session of the 10th of June. He talks about the current security situation and the tasks that the Socialist Party of Serbia and the state organs face in the process of the further improvement of the situation in Kosovo and Metohija. In the debate --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just a moment. Before that, in paragraph 2, does he not say that that anti-terrorist action is over?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is his assessment that the established tasks were carried through, that the most important terrorist strongholds were successfully eliminated, and that the situation in Kosmet was getting back to normal at an accelerated pace. That practically means that the citizens were returning to their places of residence and that there were examples of massive surrender of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who was surrendering weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Citizens who were either forced by the terrorists to join them or in their activities. The conclusion was --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just another thing before the conclusion. Please look at paragraph 4 of what he was saying. It says: "He pointed out..." What was it that he pointed out?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is referred to here is the successful implementation of humanitarian activities in terms of dealing with the consequences of the activity of Albanian terrorist gangs. What is highlighted it the enormous importance of humanitarian aid for the normalisation of the situation, particularly due to the fact that it was distributed to all the citizens who needed it, irrespective of their religious, ethnic, political, or any other affiliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Finally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, where is the reference to the examples of massive surrender of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no. The witness said that himself. These are the minutes, but it's abbreviated. It's not really stenographic notes. It is paragraph 3 -- no, 4. Surrender of weapons. It is paragraph 4. You see, it says "the Executive Committee has," and then - one, two, three, four - in the fourth paragraph there, it says: "Hand-over of arms."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, who were these citizens who were handing over arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were Albanians who had joined the terrorist groups either because they had been forced to or because they wanted to participate in terrorist activities of their own accord. Otherwise, it was clear from this document that, at that point in time, the terrorists had suffered a defeat and that their activity had been rejected by the members of their very own ethnic community, and that that meant a rejection of a policy of violence, isolation, and secession that the terrorists had advocated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know how this surrender of weapons was done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This was the job of the competent organs. I know that the organs of the Ministry of the Interior called upon citizens through the media to surrender their weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've answered my question by saying you don't know how this was done. Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Finally, in the last paragraph in Milomir Minic's statement, there is a reference to the objectives of the Socialist Party of Serbia. Could you tell us something about that? It says: "Once again," and so on. It says: "He repeated." It's on page 2 at the very end.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What is reiterated here is the firm commitment of the Socialist Party of Serbia to have all problems in Kosmet resolved by political means, peacefully, without any pre-conditions, through a direct dialogue between the representatives of the Albanians and all other ethnic groups living in the province. An invitation is being proffered to have these talks start as soon as possible and to find a solution that would ensure full respect for human and civic rights and the rights of all ethnic communities. At the same time, they insisted in their views on stepping up activities for revitalising economic activities, rebuilding the infrastructure, and a very active involvement of state organs in normalisation of the situation in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, could it be said that this session was held in relation to the session of the Main Board of the Socialist Party of Serbia on the 10th of June, 1998? Are they related? Is there any link there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Practically, this session represented a report and a summary of what was done pursuant to the conclusions of -- reached at the session of the Main Board on the 10th of June, 1998. At the same time, the speech by Milomir Minic was also a report of our team on the accomplishment of those tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did this mean that the mission of the team was accomplished?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From that time on, the team diminished its activities in Kosmet, and I think that, as a team, they attended a couple of more meetings of the party organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, they did not spend time in Kosmet on a daily basis after that, because members of the team had other engagements to attend. They would travel there sporadically, but they would not stay in Kosovo permanently any longer after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please now turn to tab 4. This is Exhibit 2D77, and that, Mr. Jovanovic, is minutes of the session of the SPS Executive Board held on the 14th of October, 1998. We're speaking of the Socialist Party of Serbia naturally. Would you please confirm the authenticity of the document, and then I will put some further questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the seal and the signature of the executive secretary, this is a document that represents the minutes of the Executive Board of the SPS.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please take a good look. Therefore, what was achieved by this session?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this session, the Socialist Party of Serbia supported the agreement reached between the President of the FRY, Slobodan Milosevic, and special envoy of the United States, Richard Holbrooke, concerning a solution to the problems in Kosovo and Metohija by way of political means. The SPS supported this document because it confirmed the validity of our political views that problems in Kosovo could only be resolved via peaceful means without the use of force and in a way that would ensure full equality of all ethnic communities. At the same time, the SPS believed that the arrival of the OSCE mission meant that the position on resolving the problems in Kosovo through political means has won the day, and that at the same time the threat of use of force was removed for good, as well as the threat of a military intervention, which would only serve to encourage the terrorists. The SPS saw a large number of observers who were experienced and who had come from a number of countries as a possibility to send to the world a message on the numbers, activities, and intentions of terrorists, a true message, and a possibility to deny the lies that had been published by some prominent international media outlets about Serbia being some sort of an aggressor in its own territory and that there was some sort of humanitarian catastrophe and the like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you learn the terms of the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How did you learn them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We learned of the terms in the speech of Milan Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you to look at the second bullet on page 3 of this document. Let me know when you're ready.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Once again, this deals with the Working Group that was designated at the 16th session of the Executive -- Main Board, comprising Minic, Andjelkovic, and Matkovic. What was their mission?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their mission was to continue their work with the provincial council of -- or rather, Provincial Board of the SPS for Kosovo and Metohija, to get involved in explaining the agreement and its importance for preserving peace and improving the situation in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So this is the session of the board that you spoke of yesterday that they attended?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know when it was held?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was held at the end of the month, and I think that, practically speaking, that was the last time they stayed there as a team. As a team, as individuals, they had a task to give statements to the media later on about the agreement, to talk of its importance, to explain to the public and to the citizens the terms of the agreement and its importance for implementing our political views.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So that was the end of the work of this group in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is when their activities in Kosovo and Metohija ceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, would you please turn to tab 5. This is Defence Exhibit 2D88. Once again, these are minutes dated the 27th of October, 1998, the minutes of the session of the Executive Board of the SPS. Would you please confirm the authenticity of the document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by the signature of the main secretary and -- or rather, General-Secretary and the seal, these are authentic minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now would you please turn to page 3, item 2, and let me know when you're ready.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What can we see in item 2 here?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this session, they analysed the implementation of the said agreement. In essence, they insisted on having all state organs take a very serious and active attitude towards implementation of the tasks within their competence, which would mean -- or rather, which would amount to meeting all of the obligations as established by the agreement. It is important to point out that here, we can see that the party in its position insisted that its members in the state organs commence a serious and responsible implementation of the tasks immediately, so that our side would meet all of its obligations pursuant to the agreement. This position that I just described is not contained in the communique that is part of this agreement. Based on that, you can see that this was no method of pleasing the media; rather, this is a well-formulated position of the SPS that the entire agreement had to be implemented, and that our members who held senior posts in state organs needed not to wait for any additional instructions but, rather, needed to proceed with implementation of the agreement in its entirety within their sphere of competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was there any mention of members of the Albanian ethnic minority and the need to have them involved in all activities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is mention of that, and that was a well-known position of the party that was formulated in all of our documents. Here they additionally insisted on using the improved situation in Kosovo to involve all citizens, especially members of ethnic minorities in all political activities, to step up efforts to achieve political dialogue in order to find a solution that would satisfy everybody, and to make sure that this process is accelerated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where do we see that in the minute, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is item 3, item 3 on page 3. Let's me see the translation. In the English translation on page 3, somewhere in the middle of that page, it says that he pointed out, or rather, emphasised -- stressed the importance of increasing and strengthening of the Serbian national body and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What does that mean, Mr. Jovanovic, "stressed importance of increasing and strengthening the Serbian national body in Kosovo"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This means encouraging citizens who are ethnic Serbs to not leave their villages, their homes, and their land in Kosovo and Metohija. This means encouraging them to establish some form of dialogue with their neighbours. What this also means is providing them with a reply to their great concern caused by the terrorist threats of making Kosovo and Metohija secede.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please go to page 3, under (B). We spoke about this a while ago, but could you please explain, again, what this is about. There are some tasks mentioned there.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In practical terms, what we see here is this team appointed at the 16th session of the Main Board, and they are told to take part in the work of the Municipal Board of the SPS in Kosovo and Metohija. The board will review the situation in the province, and these people are to report back to the Executive Board of the SPS. As far as I know, the team attended that particular session, and their mission was over.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please now go to tab 6, Defence Exhibit 2D206. Again, minutes from the 95th session of the Executive Board of the SPS held on the 3rd of February, 1999. Could you please confirm the authenticity of this document, sir, and then have a closer look. Tell us when you're ready.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no stamp on this document, but the signature looks authentic, Gorica Gajevic's signature; therefore, I do believe that these are indeed minutes of the Executive Board. It's probably just a poor copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The copy we have looks as though it's had an illegible stamp on it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the original stamp was not particularly legible. These are minutes of this session of the Main Board. This was a particularly important session of the Main Board -- of the Executive Board. I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said it yourself, didn't you, this was a very important session of the Executive Board. I would like to ask you to explain briefly and comment on the subject matter being discussed here. We see that this deals with Rambouillet. So what is the position taken by the Executive Board in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This session is devoted to briefing a delegate group from the Socialist Party of Serbia for an extraordinary session of the Socialist Party of Serbia at which they were supposed to discuss preparations for the Rambouillet talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was the position taken by the Executive Board of the SPS, specifically?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this session of the Executive Board, there was intense, ongoing consultations with representatives of parliamentary political parties in their delegates clubs aimed at formulating a joint political position. Our own position, the position espoused by the SPS, was that one had to go to Rambouillet. There was no choice but to go and participate in the talks since this was another opportunity for us to defend our political positions internationally and, yet again, try to advocate a peaceful political solution for Kosovo to be achieved by political means, by direct dialogue between the parties involved. All of this done in a way that would make sure human rights were secured for everyone, as well as equal rights for all the ethnic communities there. This position was adopted despite fact that the invitation to Rambouillet in terms of the way it was sent, in terms of how the meeting was organised, in terms of the 15-day deadline given for a resolution to this age-old problem, and, eventually, in terms of the threat being made in the eventuality there was no agreement, the threat of aggression against our country. This was, in actual fact, an ultimatum. The SPS understood full well that all they were looking for was a "casus belli," a good reason to go to war, to launch an intervention in Kosovo and Metohija, and that is why our commitment was to go to Rambouillet to do the talks, and meanwhile to try to achieve a full political consensus and unity in the Assembly, in order to build a joint platform for the formulation of our policies during the talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: About the objective --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One things needs clarified. In page 19, line 13, this is said to be "a session devoted to briefing a delegate group from the Socialist Party of Serbia for an extraordinary session of the Socialist Party of Serbia." Now, I think it's "extraordinary session of the national assembly," but I think we should get from the interpreters in due course, whenever they get a chance to listen to the tape again, what exactly was said. Can I ask you, Mr. Jovanovic, this was a fairly brief meeting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The meeting didn't take long, given the fact that political contacts with other political parties were fairly intense at the time, in terms of preparing the national assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was it more or less a formality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was far from being a formality. This was an exceptionally important session. Our political position was crystal clear and had been adopted at previous sessions; therefore, we didn't run ourselves ragged just talking. We simply tried as hard as we could to prepare the session of the national assembly in the best possible way. The Executive Board is an operative body for the implementation of policies. Sometimes long meetings are not required, although politicians seem to have a knack to hold long meetings and talk at great length.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As far as I understand you, sir, the aim was to avoid the pretext for war and also to put our case to the world; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By all means. If I may, we had every confidence that the Contact Group would mean a step forward, and that, in Rambouillet, we would be facing directly the representatives of the Albanian community which had thus far not been the case. We believed that, through a direct dialogue, we could get things started and start looking for solutions that would suit both sides equally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know if the tape recording of this meeting is available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, Your Honour, just a brief explanation. Each session of the Executive Board and each session of the Main Board were tape recorded. There were tapes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not according to the earlier minutes that we've been looking at. It specifically says in them that they were not recorded, so I simply wondered if the tape of this one was available.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It only happened very rarely that a meeting was not recorded, and, normally, this occurred for technical reasons. If anything was recorded, the tapes should be there. However, the tapes were kept in a building that was, unfortunately, bombed during the NATO aggression, but we can still go back to the headquarters of the SPS and make requests to see if any of these tapes have been preserved. I was not a member of the Main Board of the SPS after 2000; therefore, I'm not in a position to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So all tapes were lost, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When this happened, I was still working as a secretary to the Technical Services unit. Not only were the tapes destroyed, but also the best part of all other documents, documents of various kinds. Most of the archives belonging to the Main Board of the SPS were destroyed on two separate occasions when the building was bombed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were all the financial records destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some of the records were moved at the beginning of the aggression to the headquarters of the town board, the city board of the Socialist Party of Serbia, and this batch included financial records. However, on the 5th of October, the demonstrators twice broke into the building of the Main Board, looted the building, and threw out the window whatever they could, including the cash desk that weighed several hundreds kilogrammes. Twice they set fire to the building, and the fire brigade had to step in. There is a police record what was drawn up about this and about the fact that financial records and other documents belonging to the SPS that were kept in the building were destroyed on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that would be the 5th of October, 2000?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 7th, the 8th, it was at that time, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The minutes, though, have survived in their entirety, have they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The minutes and the tapes were not kept in the same place. Apart from that, the minutes were distributed to all members of the Executive Board. It was very easy to obtain copies of these documents because everybody kept it in their own personal archives, but not everybody preserved the minutes from these sessions. The minutes were used only if there were objections to be raised about the minutes themselves so that the tapes might then be consulted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know the source of the ones we've been referring to today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know where these minutes came from. I suppose they were obtained from the Main Board and the Executive Board of the Socialist Party of Serbia when this trial first started.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can be of assistance, I'm the one who obtain the minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you wish to tell me from where you obtained them?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the now president of the SPS, Ivica Dacic. I phoned him and I went there to get the minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You went to the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you had a point to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, page 23, 23, lines 15 through 21, the minutes are mentioned there and the witness is talking about the tapes; therefore, I think the witness should be asked to explain the distinction between the minutes and the tapes. I don't think the distinction is clear in these lines, and I think this is essential for the understanding of what the witness is talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the distinction, as I see it, is that what we have are minutes. That's a typewritten record in abbreviated form of what transpired at the meeting, and the tape will be a verbatim record of all that happened at the meeting, and I think the distinction's clear there. Please continue, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you now please go to tab 10, sir. This is Defence Exhibit, 1D443.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the Official Gazette is, and then we can take it from there.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Official Gazette of the Republic of Serbia is a printed media belonging to the state. Under our constitution, all enactments by state bodies must be published in the Official Gazette; all of the government enactments, all of the judicial enactments, and such like. This is a publication in which original laws and regulations published by -- adopted by state organs are published.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So what is the distinction between the Official Gazette Sluzbeni List and Sluzbeni Glasnik.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sluzbeni List is the Official Gazette of the Republic of Serbia, and Sluzbeni Glasnik is the Official Gazette of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. So this one is the Official Gazette of the Republic of is Serbia. There are some conclusions there. Could you please not read them out loud. We might be dead by the time you finish. Just comment please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Briefly, this document is a political platform and a mandate for the delegation of the Republic of Serbia at the Rambouillet talks. In the introductory part, the Assembly condemns all threats of NATO aggression. They reiterate the principles that we see as a potential solution: For the umpteenth time, peace, political means, direct dialogue averting any threats of force and insistence on human and civil rights as defined by international standards, as well as equal rights for all ethnic communities in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does this give a mandate to our delegation that went there; and if so, what is the mandate?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our delegation -- our delegation had a mandate to achieve a political solution within the principles established by the National Assembly of Serbia. It is with that mandate that the delegation was sent to the Rambouillet talks. The conclusions contained general principles. So the delegation, on the one hand, had a clear mandate, and, on the other hand, sufficient manoeuvering space for seeking institutional solutions in direct dialogue that would move within the framework of the principles set by the national assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you to look at tab 7, Defence Exhibit number 2D218. You have to go back a bit, one back.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did you say tab 7?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Tab 7. This is the minutes of the 96th session of the SPS Executive Board held on the 17th of February, 1999. I would like to ask you first to confirm the authenticity of this document. It bears a signature and a stamp. And could you have a look at it; and when you're ready, I'd like to put some questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are authentic minutes of a meeting of the Executive Board. It's all right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If I see correctly, on the first page, it says that Nikola Sainovic is not present; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Nikola Sainovic did not attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you something more important than that. Could you tell us something in relation to these minutes. What was the subject that was discussed at this meeting of the Executive Board, and what was the position taken by the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this session, the Executive Board was informed about how the talks in Rambouillet were proceeding, aimed at resolving the problems in Kosovo and Metohija. The essence of this information pertains to rendering support to our delegation that was at the Rambouillet talks, so that they would persevere along the principles established by the national assembly of the Republic of Serbia. This position is not merely a confirmation of policy, but it is being repeated because of the awareness that our delegation was exposed to pressures to accept solutions that were not an integral part of the plan when the talks in Rambouillet were originally scheduled. It is precisely for that reason that, on page 4, the Executive Board assesses that constant threats of a NATO aggression, especially issued by the United States of America, actually instigate terrorists in the field and, on the other hand, keep the Albanian side even farther away from discussing a political solution, and that is what the conference had been called for in Rambouillet. At that point in time, our political positions are actually being re-interpreted, and a willingness is being achieved in Rambouillet itself and to have talks started practically through direct dialogue with the expectation that the negotiators would indeed abide by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was the position regarding equality of rights repeated as well, the equality of rights of all ethnic communities, autonomy, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. That is a constant feature of our policy and, therefore, it is contained in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that this would be an appropriate moment to take the break, because I think that our work schedule is shorter today, isn't it? Yet another day when you did not keep your promise that you would give me more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You leave me at a loss for words, Mr. Fila. Someone, some day will tell you the efforts that have been made. Mr. Jovanovic, we have to have a break at this stage. It will be for 20 minutes. The usher will take you from the court now and show you where you can wait, and we will resume at 10.50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, we went through quite a few documents of the Executive Board. So far it has become obvious that you repeated several times that what is discussed is a political solution, that that is what the Executive Board is advocating, a political solution on the basis of the equality of rights of all ethnic communities and highest standards for autonomy. All these positions that you talked about this morning, were they also turned into documents; and if so, were they presented to the representatives of the Kosovo Albanians and the international community?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to your question is yes. They were turned into two concrete documents. The first one is called the "Joint Agreement on Political Frameworks for Self-government in Kosovo and Metohija" from November 1998, and the second one is entitled the "Agreement on Self-government in Kosmet," dated the 15th of March, the year after that, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Pause briefly, please, and let us have a look at these documents. Please look at tab 12. That is 1D91. Please look at it carefully; and when you're ready, signal me so I can put my questions.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So what kind of a document of is this? Tell us a bit about that, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document that was drafted through broad consultations with the representatives of ethnic communities of the Turks, the Gorani, the Muslims, the Roma, Egyptians, Serbs; then, with the participation of parliamentary political parties, the Socialist Party of Serbia, the Serb Radical Party, the Serbian Renewal Movement, New Democracy, the alliance of the Vojvodina Hungarians, and the Yugoslav Left.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In relation to the transcript, Your Honours, all of this is being recorded as my question, but it is actually from line 13 onwards the witness's answer. So could that please be corrected. All of it is registered as my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, please go on now.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for all the participants in the drafting and consultations related to this paper, generally speaking, you can see that it was broadly supported by the opposition parties in Serbia as well. At the same time, this document was supported by the People's Party of Kosovo and the Kosovo Democratic Initiative, two smaller parties from Kosmet. In actual fact, this is a paper that very specifically elaborates the principles involved, not only of guaranteeing and exercising human and civil rights in terms of self-government in Kosovo, but also additional rights for members of ethnic communities in Kosmet. The document went beyond repeating principles; namely, it established what the rights involved were in -- namely, how organs would be constituted, how they would function. And at the same time, it was not a self-contained paper; it was an offer to the Albanian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What did it actually envisage? Could you please tell us in greater detail, because this is a very important document regarding the position of Serbia at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The essence of this paper is to establish full equality of rights of all ethnic communities in a way which would prevent the possibility of having any ethnic community being out-voted in relation to some other ethnic community or another group of ethnic communities. It was done in the following way: A special procedure of decision-making was envisaged for the Assembly that would protect the rights of ethnic communities if they would believe that their right was being threatened.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In what way?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was elaborated in greater detail in other document but in a way that envisages a special decision-making process in such cases, not allowing for majority votes in the Assembly with regard to such issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We'll get to that later.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It also refers to the rights of citizens in terms of local government in municipalities that are the basic units of local self-government. What is particularly emphasised is the representation of citizens of Kosovo and Metohija in federal and republican organs, which shows that we always built a political platform so that the citizens of Kosovo would take part in the republican and federal authorities by ensuring their proper representation in the legislation, in the executive, and in the top organs of the judiciary: The Federal Court, for instance; three judges on the Supreme Court; in the Chamber of Citizens of the then-Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, there were supposed to be at least ten seats for MPs; and in the national assembly, 20 seats for MPs from the territory of this autonomous province of ours. On the other hand, this paper also meant the elaboration of the funds needed to ensure self-government or self-role. It also established new responsibilities for organs, and it provided possibilities for the republic and the federal state to provide additional funds for the functioning of provincial organs. So it also contained measures forbidding confidence among citizens and ethnic communities, and those were very specific measures aimed at overcoming any separation and creation of parallel institutions that would not be condusant [as interpreted] to the entire idea. We wanted to prevent the creation of apartheid, and we wanted to encourage the ethnic communities to resolve jointly all of the problems they had in Kosovo. This paper also specified that no one would be subject to criminal Prosecution for their activities in Kosovo and Metohija and also measures for the implementation of the agreement. So this was a joint platform, joint position of the signatories, and it was not accepted only by the representatives of ethnic Albanians; rather, it was not supported by the major political parties. It was supported by two minor Albanian political parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If I understood you well, other ethnic minorities such as Hungarians and others throughout Serbia supported this agreement.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: See here, we had a very strong opposition in the National Assembly of Serbia at that time. It was personified in the then most influential political party, which was the Serbian Renewal Movement. That party fully approved of this document and provided very firm support to it by way of various official statements, official announcements, and speeches given by their chairman, Vuk Draskovic, through various interviews and so on. They explained that the majority of the people in Kosovo and Metohija supported this agreement, because representatives of various ethnic communities, together with a number of Albanians who supported this document, did represent the majority. Other parties such as the New Democracy and the Alliance of Vojvodina Hungarians also participated in elaboration of these solutions, and they supported this approach and this method of finding a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let us turn to tab 13. This is 2D384, Defence exhibit. This is this other document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document, unfortunately, has no translation, because we obtained it in our additional interview with the witness. The Prosecution has been notified. They raised no objections in relation to using this document. We sent this document to the Translation Unit. This witness took part in drafting this document -- this document. And I would like you to mark it for identification later on, and for the time being I'll just ask the witness to comment on the document. And could it be marked for identification, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can decide that once we've completed the questions on that, on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please look at 2D384, tab 13. Since we don't have it in English, Mr. Jovanovic, I will put questions to you and then you can either point to various portions of the text or read them out, the portions that corroborate your answers.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How does this agreement ensure equality of ethnic communities that you spoke of? And before that, let me ask you what document is this, and tell us something about how it was created, when, and so on, and then proceed to the question that I put to you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is entitled "Agreement on Self-government in Kosmet." It was signed in Paris on the 15th of March by the delegation of the Republic of Serbia, headed by Professor Ratko Markovic and representatives of ethnic communities, Albanians -- ethnic communities of Albanians, Roma, Serbs, and Montenegrins, Turks, Muslims, and Egyptians. The delegation signed this document in Paris, and it was submitted to the negotiators and to the Albanian side, which refused to sign it. The document itself was also distributed to the assemblymen of the National Assembly of Serbia, and they accepted it and supported our delegation. Unlike previous documents which elaborated principles for the solution, this document was quite specific about a number of institutional modalities, ensuring the equality of ethnic communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Before you proceed, I'd like to know whether you were present in Paris when this was drafted, and how did you contribute to the drafting of the document, if at all?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present in Paris when this document was signed in the capacity of an advisor to some of the ethnic communities. In addition to that, I was also consulted when the document was drafted concerning the portions about the election system and the National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. You can proceed now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we be more specific, Mr. Fila, or do you just want the witness to ramble through the document and select what he wants to tell us about, or are you going to focus the questions on what really matters here?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will. I just wanted to establish that he was present and that he was there when the document was signed, just to confirm that the document is authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What is important here is the question that I have already put to you; namely, how does this document ensure the equality of ethnic communities that you spoke of?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most prominent aspect of ensuring equality of ethnic communities is a right that can be found in item 6 of Article 1 of the Principles of the Self-government in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please read it out since we don't have the text in English.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will. "Every ethnic community, in order to protect national or ethnic features, and based on the approval of its members, can specify special rules such as in the area of marriage, family, adoption, guardianship, and probate."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This is chapter 1 of the main document; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what does this actually mean for the Muslims in practical terms?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For Muslims, specifically, this means that in these areas, such as family relations, marriage relations, probate and so on, that all of these areas could be regulated in accordance with the Sharia [Realtime transcript read in error "Saraja"] law; and if members of that community accepted that, then these relations would be regulated in accordance with the laws established by the ethnic community. The scope of the areas that could be regulated by provisions of ethnic communities was broader than just those enumerated here, because each ethnic community could specify that the number of these areas would be greater than those mentioned in the law regulating this area. This is quite a unique approach, unique in the world. This is the greatest amount of freedom given to ethnic minorities, national minorities, that was ever proposed, and it illustrates just how far we were prepared to go to ensure equality of ethnic communities in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In line 14 of the transcript, the reference is there is "Sharia" law. That's S-h-a-r-i-a. Please continue, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. You can see that we have consultations here at the Defence table. It seems that we have this document in English, and we're now trying to locate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you now just look at Article II of this document, which speaks about the organisation of the Assembly of Kosovo and Metohija. How was this Assembly supposed to function?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: II, Article II, Roman II. Here we can see what was done in order to ensure ethnic equality by means of institutions. First of all, the Assembly of Kosmet was supposed to have 130 members. Out of that number, 95 members were supposed to be elected by way of a proportional voting system in Kosmet being considered one electoral unit in accordance with all the standards normally governing democratic elections. Thirty-five members were supposed to be elected by ethnic communities. Each was accorded five seats. The Assembly was supposed to vote by majority on the greatest number of issues. However, when it came to issues which, in view of certain ethnic communities, could threaten their national identity, a special decision-making system was envisaged. This system amounted to the following: At least three members of a particular ethnic community could ask that a special procedure be applied to adopt certain decisions, if they believed that their ethnic interest was at stake. In order to prevent abuse of this right, the document was very clear about the specific cases where such special decision-making system could be requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And those were?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were election of organs of Kosmet to equal national representation in all organs when it came to displacement of citizens if their security was threatened and if it involved, say, a budget.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What were the responsibilities of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were quite broad; but, in this case, the president of the Assembly would institute a special decision-making system where a consensus of all sides was required. The substance of this particular approach was to prevent any out-voting of any ethnic community by another ethnic community. See here, the Assembly was supposed to vote decisions by majority on the greatest number of questions; and only when it came to questions that dealt with preserving national identity, there was a special system where voting was by consensus on a very limited number of issues. The Albanian community was against this system of voting by majority in Serbia. But when it came to themselves in Kosmet, they wanted this particular system to be applied; namely, voting by majority. All other ethnic communities were worried that this decision-making system would condemn them to assimilation, to being constantly out-voted, and to have their rights threatened as well as their national identity. This is exactly why we came up with this solution when it came to the work of the Assembly, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please go to Article V, item 2, paragraph 1. This is about courts in Kosovo. How were these to be organised?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the judicial system, this principle of protecting ethnic minorities was brought to its ultimate conclusion. We would have Serbian courts in Kosovo and Metohija, courts set up by Kosovo's self-government, as well as courts established by the ethnic minorities. Paragraph 2 says that: "Citizens and all other legal subjects in Kosovo would have the right to be tried by a court of their own choosing. Each citizen or legal person in their capacity as prosecutor, proposer, or accused have the right to choose whether he would be tried by a Serbian court."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: On account of your speed, I don't think this was properly recorded. Perhaps you should start over.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. I'll try to speak slowly. Paragraph 2 of Article V says that: "Citizens and legal persons have the right to choose before which court they want to be tried or start any proceedings within civil law -- in civil cases and criminal cases." What this means is that the citizens of a particular ethnic community could choose to be tried by a court established by their own ethnic community, by judges from the ranks of their ethnicity, and by prosecutors belonging to their own ethnic community. It was in this way that one tried to prevent the possibility of the judicial system being used by one ethnic community for its own purposes, or the possibility of legal proceedings being used in favour of a specific ethnic community. Needless to say, this procedure would be used quite liberally. It was not a compulsory procedure. Parties to a proceedings had a choice between three different courts as a potential venue for their legal actions. One of these options was the court set up by the Republic of Serbia, then the self-government in Kosovo, or, thirdly, their own ethnic community. This is an extremely democratic and functional solution, and all of the other national ethnic communities accepted this solution and backed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What would happen, Mr. Jovanovic, if a Kosovo Albanian murdered a Serb? Where would that person be tried?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the parties fail to reach an agreement as to which court would be their venue of choice, then the document said nothing about that. However, this is just a framework document. It was not a take it or leave it document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's only one party in that situation, the alleged killer who can be choose to be tried by a Kosovo Albanian court according to your evidence so far. Is that realistic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is realistic, because there's always the other side, the prosecutor. What I said is this: This paper, this document, is not self-contained. It's not a cut-and-dried solution. It offers a variety of solutions to these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. You've told us also that the person accused can choose his own prosecutor, if I have understood you properly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The document says that the person can choose his own prosecutor as being a prosecutor nominated by the republic, Kosovo's self-government, or the person's own ethnic community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In our system, is there just the accused or is there also the damaged party and the prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, the other side in our system is the prosecutor, the prosecutor who ex officio prosecutes potential criminals. However, even this shows to what degree we were ready to push this just to ensure equal rights for all ethnic communities. And one thing that one must bear in mind is that the citizens in Kosmet and the ethnic minorities did not trust the bodies of the province. The bodies of the province, the legislative bodies and the judicial bodies, had no credibility among the population and no authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was this an attempt to deal with that situation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly was. What we wanted to do, in actual fact, was to start at the general legal principles and work from there in order to find political and institutional models that would be operational in practice. His Honour Judge Bonomy is entirely right when he claims that these models are complex and that it would be difficult to get them up and running and for them to start functioning properly, but it's better to have complex and expensive models than to create dissatisfaction among the ethnic communities, because it was the divisions between the ethnic communities that led to the sort of intolerance that in its turn was to lead to open conflict. We were convinced that by offering solutions of this nature we were building bridges between the different ethnic communities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, what were the legislative bodies that the citizens did not trust?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The citizens did not trust bodies that were established in line with the majority principle, because in that case, at the level of the province itself, the Albanians would be majority, and they were afraid that in this way they would end up being out-voted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But my question is: What are the legislative bodies to which you are referring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, above all, the Assembly of the autonomous province of Kosovo, which because of its illegal and unconstitutional actions was finally dissolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you're talking about the lack of trust by non-Albanian ethnic minorities and Serbs in the previous Kosovo Assembly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please open tab 11 now, sir. Defence document 1D114. While you're looking for it - that's the one - are you familiar with this letter by representatives of the ethnic communities in Kosovo, the letter that they sent to those holding talks in Paris?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of this letter. This is the letter that representatives of the ethnic communities sent to the co-chairmen of the Rambouillet conference, Mr. Vedrine and Mr. Cook. In this letter, they draw the co-chairmen's attention to the fact that the negotiating troika of Hill, Petritsch, and Mayorski did not show enough understanding for their suggestions, suggestions which they believed should be part of the final document. They also admonish the negotiators, the co-chairmen, that during the Rambouillet talks, the Rambouillet conference, what was practically abandoned was exactly what had been agreed in the principles of the Contact Group on the 29th of January, 1999. At the same time, they draw attention to the fact that the proposed document favoured the Albanian ethnic community because of the introduction of the majority principle in establishing the various institutions, and that the rights and the position of all the remaining ethnic communities were being entirely neglected, and these numbered at least 600.000. They also underline the fact that there is a number of different ethnic communities living in Kosovo and Metohija, and that merely invoking civil and human rights without offering additional instruments to protect the rights of ethnic minorities in practical terms leaves them with no choice but to leave Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This brings us to the end of this particular subject. I would like to tender this document, although it was not translated, 2D384. I would like to tender that to be marked for identification until we have received final translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Has the investigation into the idea that there's an English version somewhere been completed?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, but it resulted in nothing at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. This document will be marked for identification. That's 2D384.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm now moving on to my last subject. Could you go to tab 9, sir, please. I'm taking you back now. Professor, we shall discuss Mr. Nikola Sainovic, who is my client before this Tribunal. Could you look at tab 9, please. What does this document show? What is this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the results of the elections at the Congress of the Socialist Party of Serbia. At this Congress, Mr. Nikola Sainovic was appointed deputy president.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The document number is P2875. It's an OTP document.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document showing exactly which bodies were elected at this Congress. Among them, we see Mr. Nikola Sainovic being elected vice-president. He's followed by members of the Main Board and those of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When was the Congress held?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In March 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Fine. Can you now please go back to tab 1. The document is 2D25. It's a Defence exhibit. Have a close look, sir, please, and tell us when you're ready. May I ask my question first?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Are these minutes, minutes of what exactly, and what is the date?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are minutes from the 10th session of the Main Board of the Socialist Party of Serbia, held on the 24th of April, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So what was the fate of Mr. Nikola Sainovic, the party's vice-president, at least based on these minutes at page 3?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this session, he was replaced and dismissed from his post as vice-president of the SPS.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At whose proposal? Does the record show that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One can see here that this was done at the proposal of President Slobodan Milosevic. Formerly, the decision is taken by the Main Board, which is perfectly in keeping with the statute. The president had the sole right of making proposals for the post of the vice-president to the Main Board. It follows that he also had the right to make proposals regarding their dismissal from that post.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, Mr. Nikola Sainovic was dismissed at the proposal of Slobodan Milosevic; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You understood me well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why was Nikola Sainovic replaced?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously, he had not met expectations in carrying out the work assigned to him by the president of the SPS. I am not familiar with the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: After this dismissal from the post of vice-president of the party, did Nikola Sainovic, nevertheless, keep some position in party, and why was that the case? I would like you to explain to me why he was not completely expelled.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, he remained a member of the Executive Board of the Main Board of the Socialist Party, and that was a degradation de facto from a high office held by an individual. He was relegated to a collective organ. He did remain in the executive organ, I think, because he had good results in the elections. For the party, this regional influence is important for their own rating in the elections. As far as I can remember, in the last elections, in the year 2000 that had been lost by President Milosevic, Nikola Sainovic in his district won half of the mandate for SPS. Four seats -- four seats were provided by that district, and he won two for his party.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now that we've gone into the field of politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The entire transcript from the break onwards contains many imprecisions. I don't really want to take all of this back. Could it please be listened to, the audio recording, because there are many things here that are not right. We cannot intervene each and every time. There is quite a bit of confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think what I'd like you to do, Mr. Fila, before deciding how to tackle this, is identify some examples. Now, that can be done at the break. I am concerned, obviously, about what you say, but it would help, I think, if some examples could be given to us and perhaps that would be a starting point. Anyway, we could leave it for the moment, and please proceed and continue to be vigilant for us on the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am drawing this to a close anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So, Mr. Jovanovic, since we are now dealing with the person of Nikola Sainovic, what can you tell us about Nikola Sainovic's political engagement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that he was one of the top managers in the biggest metallurgy complex in the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; that he was president of a municipality; that he held many party functions in the one-party system; that he was elected in that system as a federal deputy, federal MP; that he was Minister for Energy in the republican government, I think; then the prime minister of the Republic of Serbia; the deputy federal prime minister; and, from 1996, he was elected president -- vice-president of the SPS at the 3rd Congress. It is believed that at that Congress a so-called softer line of politicians was elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
